Pushing two bodies together **against** a repulsive force means doing work on them, and
that work is stored as potential energy.
**Step 1 — see which way the force acts.** Two protons carry like charges, so the
Coulomb force between them is **repulsive** - each pushes the other away ✓
**Step 2 — see what bringing them closer requires.** Moving them together means pushing
**against** that repulsion, so an external agent must do **positive work** ✓
**Step 3 — follow the energy.** That work does not disappear. It is stored in the system
as **electrostatic potential energy**, so
**the potential energy increases** ✓
**The formula.** For two point charges,
U = kq₁q₂/r
With both charges positive, U is **positive** and grows as r shrinks ✓ As r → 0, U → ∞,
which is why two protons can never be pushed completely together by electrostatic means
alone.
**A numerical illustration.** Two protons at 10⁻¹⁰ m:
U = (9 x 10⁹)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)²/10⁻¹⁰ = **2·3 x 10⁻¹⁸ J ≈ 14 eV**
and at 10⁻¹⁵ m, a nuclear distance, U = **1·4 MeV** ✓ a hundred thousand times greater.
**Why this matters in nuclear fusion.** That rising potential energy is the **Coulomb
barrier** ✓ Two protons must be given about an MeV of kinetic energy - or helped by
quantum tunnelling, as in the Sun - before the short-range nuclear attraction can take
over and bind them.
**The general rule.** Moving **against** a force raises the potential energy; moving
**with** it lowers the potential energy ✓ That is why gravitational PE rises when a body
is lifted, and why the PE of two **opposite** charges **falls** as they approach.
**Reading the distractors.** **Decreases** ✗ is what happens for an **attractive** force,
such as between a proton and an electron. **Remains unchanged** ✗ would mean the work
done went nowhere. **May increase or decrease** ✗ - with a purely repulsive force the
sign is fixed ✓
∴ increases.

Set the potential energy gained equal to the kinetic energy already possessed.
**Step 1 — write the condition.**
mgh = ½mv²
**Step 2 — cancel the mass and solve.**
h = v²/(2g) ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
h = (20)²/(2 x 10)
= 400/20
= **20 m** ✓
**Why the mass does not appear.** Both energies are proportional to m, so it cancels ✓
A feather and a cannonball moving at 20 m s⁻¹ must each be lifted the same 20 m to gain
potential energy equal to their kinetic energy.
**What the height means physically.** 20 m is exactly how high the body would rise if
thrown **vertically upward** at 20 m s⁻¹ ✓ at the top of that rise all its kinetic energy
has turned into potential energy - precisely the condition stated.
**A check by kinematics.**
v² = u² − 2gh
0 = 400 − 20h
**h = 20 m** ✓ the same answer without mentioning energy at all.
**The coincidence of the numbers.** With v = 20 and g = 10, v²/2g = 400/20 = 20 - so the
answer happens to equal the speed ✓ That is a numerical accident of these particular
values, not a general rule: at 30 m s⁻¹ the height would be 45 m, not 30.
**Reading the distractors.** **200 m** ✗ uses v² x g/... some factor of ten astray.
**2 m** ✗ is a hundredfold too small. **2000 m** ✗ is v²x 5 ✓ A quick order-of-magnitude
check settles it: a body at 20 m s⁻¹ is travelling at 72 km/h, and such a body plainly
cannot coast two kilometres upward.
**The formula to remember.** **h = v²/2g** - the height a speed is "worth", and the same
relation that governs braking distance, projectile range and escape problems ✓
∴ 20 m.

Friction opposes motion, so the work done against it comes out of the body's **kinetic**
energy.
**Step 1 — see where the energy comes from.** Friction acts opposite to the direction of
motion, so it does **negative work** on the body ✓ By the work-energy theorem,
W_net = ΔKE
a negative work means the kinetic energy **falls**.
**Step 2 — see what happens to that energy.** It is not destroyed; it becomes **heat** in
the two rubbing surfaces, and a little sound ✓ This is why brakes get hot and why rubbing
one's hands warms them.
**Step 3 — ask about potential energy.** Friction acts **along** the surface, which is
perpendicular to the direction in which height changes ✓ It does not alter the body's
position in a gravitational or elastic field, so the **potential energy is unaffected**.
**Step 4 — conclude.** Only the kinetic energy is lost ✓
**A worked instance.** A 2 kg block slides along a level floor at 5 m s⁻¹ with μ = 0·2
and stops after 6·4 m:
work against friction: 0·2(2)(9·8)(6·4) = **25 J**
kinetic energy lost: ½(2)(25) = **25 J** ✓ exactly equal
potential energy change: **zero**, since the floor is level ✓
**The subtlety worth noting.** A block sliding **down** a rough incline loses potential
energy too - but that loss is caused by **gravity**, not by friction ✓ Friction's own
contribution is always and only to the kinetic energy, and the question asks what the
work against friction results in.
**Why friction is called non-conservative.** The energy it takes cannot be recovered by
reversing the motion ✓ Push the block back and friction takes energy again, in the other
direction - unlike gravity or a spring, which give back everything they take.
**Reading the distractors.** **Potential energy** ✗ is unchanged by a force acting along
the direction of travel. **Both of them** ✗ and **none of them** ✗ follow from the same
error ✓
∴ kinetic energy.

Work against friction is the frictional force times the distance over which it acts.
**Step 1 — find the normal force.** The surface is horizontal, so
N = mg
= (50)(9·8)
= **490 N**
**Step 2 — find the frictional force.**
f = μN
= 0·2 x 490
= **98 N**
**Step 3 — find the work done against it.**
W = f x d
= 98 x 1
= **98 J** ✓
**Why the work is positive here.** "Work done **against** friction" is the energy
expended overcoming it ✓ Friction itself does **−98 J** of work on the block; the two
statements describe the same 98 J from opposite sides.
**Where that energy goes.** All 98 J becomes **heat** at the sliding interface ✓ Enough
to raise a gram of iron by about 220 °C, if it were all concentrated there - which is why
sliding surfaces need lubrication.
**Why the surface being horizontal matters.** It makes N = mg exactly ✓ On an incline at
angle θ the normal force would be mg cos θ, and the friction correspondingly smaller.
**A check by deceleration.** The friction gives the block
a = f/m = 98/50 = **1·96 m s⁻²** of deceleration
and over 1 m that removes ½mv² = **98 J** of kinetic energy ✓ consistent with the work
calculated.
**The formula in one line.** **W = μmgd** for a horizontal surface ✓ Here
0·2 x 50 x 9·8 x 1 = 98 J, and recognising that compact form saves the intermediate
steps.
**Reading the distractors.** **72 J** ✗, **56 J** ✗ and **34 J** ✗ correspond to
coefficients of about 0·15, 0·11 and 0·07 respectively, none of them the given 0·2 ✓
Dividing any candidate by mgd = 490 recovers the implied μ and tests it at once.
∴ 98 J.

For a constant force, the work is the **dot product** of the force with the
displacement.
**Step 1 — find the displacement.**
Δr̄ = r̄₂ − r̄₁
= (14 − 3, 13 − 2, 9 − (−6))
= **(11, 11, 15)**
**Step 2 — take the dot product with the force F̄ = (4, 1, −3).**
W = F̄ · Δr̄
= 4(11) + 1(11) + (−3)(15)
= 44 + 11 − 45
**Step 3 — add.**
W = **10 units** ✓
**Watch the k̂ component.** The z displacement runs from −6 to +9, a change of **+15**,
not +3 ✓ Subtracting a negative is the step most often fumbled here, and it changes the
answer entirely.
**Watch the sign of the force's k̂ component.** It is **−3**, so that term **subtracts**
45 from the total ✓ The force opposes the motion in the z direction, taking energy back
out.
**Breaking the work down by direction.**
x: +44 - the force helps the motion
y: +11 - helps
z: −45 - **opposes** it ✓
The net is a small positive 10, because the large positive and negative contributions
nearly cancel.
**Why a dot product and not a product of magnitudes.** Only the component of the force
**along** the displacement does work ✓ The dot product performs that projection
automatically, and it correctly returns zero for a force perpendicular to the motion.
**A check on the magnitudes.**
|F̄| = √(16 + 1 + 9) = **5·10**
|Δr̄| = √(121 + 121 + 225) = **21·6**
so W = (5·10)(21·6)cos θ = 10 gives cos θ = **0·091**, that is θ = 84·8° ✓ The force is
nearly perpendicular to the displacement, which is exactly why so little work is done.
**Reading the distractors.** **50 units** ✗ ignores the negative z term. **75 units** ✗
and **200 units** ✗ arise from multiplying magnitudes or mis-signing components ✓
∴ 10 units.

The energy stored in a stretched spring is ½kx², so for the **same extension** the works
are in the ratio of the force constants.
**Step 1 — write the work done in stretching each spring.**
W₁ = ½k x²
W₂ = ½(2k) x²
the extension x being the same for both.
**Step 2 — take the ratio.**
W₁/W₂ = ½kx²/(½ x 2k x²)
= k/2k
= **1/2**
**Step 3 — state it.**
**W₁ : W₂ = 1 : 2** ✓
**Why the extension being equal is essential.** The x² cancels only because both springs
are stretched the **same distance** ✓ Had they been stretched by the same **force**
instead, the stiffer spring would extend half as far, and the works would be in the ratio
2 : 1 the other way - the opposite answer.
**Checking that other case, to see the contrast.** For the same force F:
x = F/k, so W = ½kx² = **F²/2k**
giving W₁ : W₂ = (1/k) : (1/2k) = **2 : 1** ✓ The stiffer spring then stores **less**
energy, because it barely moves.
**A numerical instance.** Take k = 100 N m⁻¹ and x = 0·1 m:
W₁ = ½(100)(0·01) = **0·5 J**
W₂ = ½(200)(0·01) = **1·0 J** ✓ a ratio of 1 : 2.
**Why the stiffer spring takes more work here.** At every stage of the stretch it resists
twice as hard, so twice the work is needed to reach the same extension ✓ The area under
the F-x graph - a triangle of height kx and base x - is simply doubled.
**The phrase "of the same material".** It is there to make the comparison fair in
appearance, but the answer depends only on k ✓ A spring's constant depends on its wire
thickness, coil radius and number of turns as well as its material.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 1** ✗ ignores the difference in stiffness. **2 : 1** ✗
is the answer to the equal-**force** version of the question - the designed trap.
**1 : 4** ✗ would need the force constants to differ by four ✓
∴ 1 : 2.

Equilibrium means the force vanishes, so differentiate the potential energy and set it
to zero.
**Step 1 — recall that force is minus the gradient of the potential energy.**
F = −dU/dx
and equilibrium requires **F = 0**, that is **dU/dx = 0**.
**Step 2 — differentiate U = a/x¹² − b/x⁶.**
dU/dx = −12a/x¹³ + 6b/x⁷
**Step 3 — set it to zero.**
12a/x¹³ = 6b/x⁷
**Step 4 — rearrange.** Multiply both sides by x¹³/6:
2a = b x⁶
x⁶ = 2a/b
**x = (2a/b)^(1/6)** ✓
**Step 5 — check that it is a stable equilibrium.** Stability needs **d²U/dx² > 0**, a
minimum of U:
d²U/dx² = 156a/x¹⁴ − 42b/x⁸
At x⁶ = 2a/b, substituting b = 2a/x⁶ gives
156a/x¹⁴ − 42(2a/x⁶)/x⁸ = 156a/x¹⁴ − 84a/x¹⁴ = **72a/x¹⁴ > 0** ✓
so U is a minimum there and the equilibrium is genuinely **stable**.
**What this potential describes.** It is the **Lennard-Jones potential**, the standard
model of the force between two neutral atoms ✓
the **1/x¹²** term is a steep short-range **repulsion**, from the overlap of electron
clouds
the **1/x⁶** term is a longer-range **attraction**, the van der Waals force ✓
The minimum between them is the **bond length** of the molecule.
**The depth of the well.** Substituting x⁶ = 2a/b back into U:
U_min = a(b/2a)² − b(b/2a) = b²/4a − b²/2a = **−b²/4a** ✓ negative, as a bound state must
be - that is the dissociation energy of the molecule.
**Reading the distractors.** **x = 0** ✗ is where U → +∞, the most unstable point
possible. **(a/2b)^(1/6)** ✗ inverts the factor of 2. **(11a/5b)^(1/6)** ✗ matches no
derivative ✓ Setting dU/dx = 0 gives 2a/b and nothing else.
∴ x = (2a/b)^(1/6).

Equal stored energies fix the ratio of the extensions; the forces then follow from
F = kx.
**Step 1 — equate the stored energies.**
½k₁x₁² = ½k₂x₂²
so
x₁²/x₂² = k₂/k₁
**x₁/x₂ = √(k₂/k₁)**
**Step 2 — write the forces.**
F₁ = k₁x₁ and F₂ = k₂x₂
**Step 3 — take the ratio and substitute.**
F₁/F₂ = (k₁/k₂)(x₁/x₂)
= (k₁/k₂)√(k₂/k₁)
= √(k₁²/k₂²) x √(k₂/k₁)
= **√(k₁/k₂)**
**Step 4 — state it.**
**F₁ : F₂ = √k₁ : √k₂** ✓
**The elegant route.** Energy can be written in terms of the force rather than the
extension:
U = ½kx² = **F²/2k**
Setting U₁ = U₂ gives F₁²/k₁ = F₂²/k₂, hence F₁/F₂ = **√(k₁/k₂)** ✓ in two lines, with no
extensions at all.
**A numerical check.** Take k₁ = 100 and k₂ = 400 N m⁻¹, with U = 2 J each:
spring 1: x₁ = √(2U/k₁) = **0·2 m**, F₁ = 100(0·2) = **20 N**
spring 2: x₂ = √(2U/k₂) = **0·1 m**, F₂ = 400(0·1) = **40 N**
ratio F₁ : F₂ = 20 : 40 = **1 : 2**, and √k₁ : √k₂ = 10 : 20 = **1 : 2** ✓ exact.
**Why the stiffer spring needs the greater force.** It stretches less for the same
energy, so to store that energy it must be pulled harder ✓ The dependence is only as the
**square root** of k, because the extension partly compensates.
**Reading the distractors.** **k₁ : k₂** ✗ would be the ratio for equal **extensions**.
**k₁² : k₂²** ✗ exaggerates the dependence. **√k₂ : √k₁** ✗ has it the wrong way round -
the numerical check above shows the **stiffer** spring takes the larger force ✓
∴ √k₁ : √k₂.
